name: Lamotrigine
sections: White to pale cream powder; very slightly soluble in water.

Patented by the Wellcome Foundation in 1980; approved for bipolar maintenance (US) in 2003. First approval/introduction: First marketed Ireland 1991; US FDA December 1994 (Wellcome Foundation / GlaxoSmithKline).

Blocks voltage-sensitive sodium channels, stabilising neuronal membranes and inhibiting release of excitatory glutamate. Receptor / target profile: Inhibits voltage-sensitive sodium and calcium channels, acting presynaptically to decrease glutamate and aspartate release.
Summary: Bioavailability ~98%; Tmax 1.4–4.8 h. ~55% protein bound. Glucuronidated in liver. Half-life ~33 h (halved by enzyme inducers, doubled by valproate).
Epilepsy – focal and generalised seizures (including tonic-clonic), Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (adjunct or monotherapy, adults and children)
Bipolar I disorder – prevention of depressive episodes
Monotherapy (adults): 25 mg once daily for 2 weeks, 50 mg once daily for 2 weeks, then increase by 50–100 mg every 1–2 weeks; usual 100–200 mg/day
With valproate: 25 mg alternate days for 2 weeks, 25 mg daily for 2 weeks; usual 100–200 mg/day
With enzyme inducers (without valproate): 50 mg daily for 2 weeks, 100 mg/day in 2 doses for 2 weeks; usual 200–400 mg/day
Bipolar: target 200 mg/day (100 mg with valproate)
Do not exceed titration schedule (rash risk); restart titration if stopped >5 half-lives
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.
Reduce maintenance dose in significant renal impairment.
Moderate/severe: reduce dose by ~25–50% (titration and maintenance).
Approved from 2 years (adjunct); rash risk higher in children.
Generally preferred over valproate when an antiepileptic is required; monitor levels as they fall during pregnancy.
Excreted in milk; monitor infant for rash and apnoea.
Serious skin rash including Stevens–Johnson syndrome/TEN – risk increased by exceeding recommended titration or with valproate; stop at first sign of rash
Cardiac conduction abnormalities (class IB activity) – caution in structural heart disease
Valproate – halve lamotrigine dose and titrate slowly
Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, rifampicin – double dose
With or without food; dispersible tablets can be dispersed in water or chewed.
Skin rash especially first 8 weeks; levels in pregnancy and with oestrogen contraceptives; ECG in structural heart disease.
Ataxia, nystagmus, seizures, coma, QRS widening. Supportive care and ECG monitoring.
SANAD (Marson et al., Lancet 2007) – lamotrigine clinically better than carbamazepine for focal epilepsy.
Calabrese et al., J Clin Psychiatry 2003 – lamotrigine delayed depressive relapse in bipolar I disorder.
Report any rash, fever or swollen glands immediately
Do not restart at full dose after a gap – consult doctor
Inform doctor about starting/stopping the pill
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
